# A simplex cap-variance bound with the larger positive vertex omitted

**Theorem.** Let T be a d-dimensional simplex, d>=2, and let a hyperplane cut its interior. Let c_i be affine heights at its vertices, with exactly two strictly positive heights p>=q>0, every other height nonpositive, and at least one height strictly negative. Let F be the fraction of the simplex in the closed captured side, and b its section's barycentric centroid. At the vertex with height p,

    F(1-F) <= d^d product_(i!=p) b_i.              (1)

If p>q the inequality is strict. If p=q, either positive vertex can be omitted and the nonstrict inequality is asserted. Arbitrarily repeated negative heights and zero-height vertices are allowed. This theorem makes no claim yet about omitting the smaller positive vertex when p>q, omitting a negative vertex, or the product of all barycentric coordinates.

## 1. Exponential section identities

Let Y_i be independent unit-rate exponential variables and V=sum c_i Y_i. The normalized vector Y/sum Y is uniform on the probability simplex and independent of its sum. Hence F=Pr(V>=0).

Let f=f_V(0)>0. The conditional section means mu_i may be defined unambiguously by coarea at V=0, or equivalently by

    mu_i=(partial F/partial c_i)/f.

They obey

    mu_i=d b_i.                                  (2)

For completeness, differentiating the uniform-simplex cap integral gives partial F/partial c_i=f_L(0)b_i, where L is the affine height on a uniform simplex point. Independence of the gamma sum gives f_V(0)=f_L(0)/d. A proper simplex section has boundary of zero relative measure and the slice difference quotients are dominated on a fixed bounded projection, so these derivatives also hold at vertex incidences.

A coefficient-zero exponential variable is independent of the event and the coarea section. Its section mean is exactly one. Deleting such coordinates leaves F and every other mu_i unchanged. Thus zero phases can be restored by multiplying the desired product by ones. In the reduced problem there are m>=1 negative coefficients -r_j<0 and two positive coefficients; its effective dimension is m+1. Identity (2) then restores exactly the original d^d product, rather than changing the dimensional factor.

## 2. Exact reduction for p>q

Write

    h=1-q/p, a_j=r_j/(q+r_j), x_j=h a_j,
    X=product_j p/(p+r_j), Y=product_j q/(q+r_j),
    rho=Y/X=product_j(1-x_j), E=1/rho-1.

All 0<x_j<h<1. Conditioning on W=sum r_jY_j and using the survival function and density of pY_p+qY_q gives

    F=(pX-qY)/(p-q)=X rho(E+h)/h,
    f=(X-Y)/(p-q).

Differentiation, or the same conditional exponential integrals, gives

    mu_q=(1-sum_j x_j/E)/h,
    mu_(negative j)=[p/(p+r_j)](1+x_j/E).

Therefore

    product_(i!=p) mu_i=(X/h)L,
    L=(1-sum_j x_j/E)product_j(1+x_j/E).           (3)

Moreover X=product_j(1-x_j/h)/rho, so

    F=(E+h)product_j(h-x_j)/h^(m+1).

Consequently the variance gap is exactly

    product_(i!=p) mu_i-F(1-F)
      =(X/h){L-rho(E+h)
                   [1-(E+h)product_j(h-x_j)/h^(m+1)]}.       (4)

The scalar expression in braces is strictly positive by the fully proved all-m theorem `candidate 31dd328861ee872c`. Since X/h>0, (4) proves the strict conclusion. No centrality assumption on b and no comparison of the other omitted-coordinate products enters this argument.

## 3. Equal positive heights and all continuity details

Fix the negative coefficients and let p decrease to q>0. The cap probabilities and section means are continuous through this limit. An elementary coarea representation shows this without differentiating a quotient with p-q in its denominator. Integrate out Y_p and put W=sum r_jY_j. On the remaining nonnegative orthant,

    Y_p=(W-qY_q)/p,
    f=(1/p) integral exp[-sum_(i!=p)Y_i-(W-qY_q)/p]
                               1_(W>=qY_q) dY_(i!=p).

The analogous integral with factor Y_i or (W-qY_q)/p gives f mu_i. On a compact positive-p interval the integrands are dominated by a constant times (1+sum Y_i)exp(-sum Y_i). The boundary W=qY_q has Lebesgue measure zero because q>0 and at least one r_j>0. Dominated convergence therefore proves continuity; the limiting f is strictly positive. The cap probability itself follows by the same argument integrating the captured event, or by bounded convergence in the original exponential variables.

Taking limits in the strict p>q inequality yields (1). When p=q, exchange of the two positive exponential variables gives mu_p=mu_q, so either can be omitted. This limit proves the nonstrict conclusion; strictness in the equal-height case is not silently inferred from strict inequalities in approximants.

Zero phases were already handled by exact independence in Section 1. The result includes closed halfspaces because proper simplex-cut boundaries have d-dimensional volume zero; the (d-1)-dimensional section centroid is still the actual one.

## 4. Exact remaining smaller-positive scalar interface

This section records an identity only. For p>q put

    B0=sum_j x_j/(1-x_j),
    C0=[(E+1)B0-E]/E.

Differentiating F in p gives

    mu_p=(1-h)C0/h,
    product_(i!=q) mu_i=(X/h)(1-h)C0
                                      product_j(1+x_j/E).   (5)

Thus the smaller-positive variance bound would require

    (1-h)C0 product_j(1+x_j/E) >= R(x,h),          (6)

with the same R as in the scalar theorem. Equation (6) is not an automatic consequence of the established larger-positive envelope: the omitted-coordinate means need not be interchangeable.

For fixed E,h and fixed product (1-x_i)(1-x_j), the left side of (6) is again a strictly concave quadratic in T=(1-x_i)+(1-x_j): B0 has a positive affine dependence T/q, and product(E+x_i) has a negative affine dependence. The right side remains affine. Therefore the same exact fixed-product extremizer lemma applies to this NEW gap, but its h-dependent prefactor changes the critical-point equations. No all-m conclusion for (6) is claimed here.
